newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus Airways needs overhaul, says new chairman.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus Airways needs overhaul, says new chairman.

text.p: National airline Cyprus Airways needs a drastic overhaul to survive future challenges, its chairman Takis Kyriakides said.

Kyriakides, recently appointed chairman of the ailing carrier, does not mince his words. He expects losses to soar as high as eight million pounds ($16.7 million) in 1997, unless things change, following an estimated loss of six million pounds in 1996.
"Something drastic must be done for Cyprus Airways to have a future," he told Reuters in an interview.
"We have had some good results in 1994 and 1995 but I feel we are not yet ready with the strategic plan that would give us the passport to the new era with success."
The state-controlled national carrier, flies a fleet of 12 Airbuses. It made pre-tax profits of 8.1 million pounds in 1994, its first profit for several years, on revenues of 137.9 million.
But profits fell by 37.5 percent in 1995 to 5.0 million pounds, and sales dropped to 130.4 million, because of rising fuel costs and a drop in tourist traffic.
Eighty percent of Cyprus Airways is state-controlled. The remaining 20 percent is traded on the Cyprus Stock Exchange.

Since mid-1996, when the first losses were announced, the company's share price has been falling, to reach a record low of 33 cents on January 16, compared with a recent high of 1.22 pounds in February 1996.
"I consider Cyprus Airways a high-risk investment. It is competing in the international environment on local terms," said one floor trader.

Kyriakides, who has publicly warned Cyprus Airways has an "expiry date" if it is not restructured, has until March to present a strategic plan to parliament on the airline's survival. In the meantime, he has some pressing problems to tackle.

Imminent deregulation of flights to and from the holiday island compromises the future of the airline. Strained labour relations have to be improved and productivity among its 2,000-strong workforce has to increase, Kyriakides said.

"It would be easy to make the arrangements for revenues and costs so we would have better results for a year or two. The difficult thing is to restructure the company in such a way that we will have a future in the long term."

Already, some 90 charter airlines ferry thousands of tourists to and from Cyprus each year. The airline's own market share, in spite of being the only local carrier, was down to 28.1 percent in 1995 from 31.2 percent in 1994. Cyprus Airways wants the pace of deregulation delayed.

"I think it is only fair for there to be a slight delay in liberalisation," said Kyriakides, referring to Cyprus's moves to harmonise its local business environment with the European Union, with which it hopes to start accession talks in roughly 12 months' time.

"Cyprus Airways must stand on its own two feet - we believe we must shape the airline to face competition and make it an airline to deal with the 21st century," said Kyriakides. "We are asking that the government not go so fast to liberalisation in order to give us the flexibility to restructure the airline."
The airline's most pressing problem is strained labour relations. Its powerful unions issued strike warnings on several occasions last year and stoppages cost the airline dearly.
Kyriakides was non-committal whether the sweeping changes would include layoffs, but said there was tremendous scope to increase productivity and keep costs down.
"It would not be correct to exclude any possibility," said Kyriakides.
He said he relies on good cooperation with the unions for the restructuring proposals to be successful, adding that they would be open to discussion with employees.
"I am sure that nobody wants the national carrier to close down and 2000 families to be affected." ($=0.47 pounds)
